texts.label: Review3.13 research framing: new sibling paragraph after first research overview
texts.text: What Is Chair Massage? Chair massage is a short massage you receive sitting up, fully clothed, in a padded portable chair that supports your chest, arms and head as you lean forward. I work through your clothing without oil, mostly on the back, shoulders, neck, arms and hands. A session usually lasts 10 to 20 minutes. The chair folds up and fits in a quiet corner, which is why chair massage is what I bring to employee appreciation days and workplace events. Most research on chair massage comes from small studies in workplaces and hospitals, usually with 15-minute sessions. In 52 employees, a 15-minute chair massage at work was followed by lower blood pressure, although the study had no comparison group. [1] In 38 nurses offered a weekly 15-minute chair massage for 10 weeks, perceived-stress scores were lower at the end. [2] In a randomized trial of 60 women on oncology nursing teams, 15-minute chair massages twice a week for three weeks were followed by lower stress scores, and less interference from pain in daily life, than no massage. [3] Studies of office workers given short chair massages over a month report less neck and back discomfort, [4] [5] and one found a higher tolerance for pressure on tender muscle points. [5] These studies are small and short. I summarize them, including the weaker results, in the research section below. Chair massage is hands-on work by a licensed massage therapist, adapted to you as you give feedback. It is not a mechanical massage chair, and studies of those devices are not included here. These are general findings, not medical advice or a promise of any result; the full summaries, including the weaker results, are in the research section below.

texts.label: Review3.13 research framing: new sibling paragraph after first research overview
texts.text: What Is Therapeutic Massage? Therapeutic massage combines focused work with time to relax. I start with what brought you in. You can ask me to stay with one area, such as your neck and shoulders, or to work more broadly, and the plan can change as you give me feedback. Research suggests that massage therapy may help reduce pain in some conditions and may improve certain movement-related outcomes in studied pain populations. [1] [2] Studies of sports massage have found small improvements in flexibility and exercise-related muscle soreness. [3] Brief massage has been studied for short-term relaxation. [4] Regular massage was associated with improved well-being in a small four-week study of older adults. [5] Some studies have looked at massage in family caregivers. [6] Research has also examined massage in relation to stress and quality-of-life measures in specific adult groups. [7] [8] [5] These are general findings, not medical advice or a promise of any result; the full summaries, including the weaker results, are in the research section below.

texts.label: Review3.13 research framing: new sibling paragraph after first research overview
texts.text: What Is Deep Tissue Massage? Deep tissue massage uses slow, deliberate pressure on muscles that stay tight. I begin by asking about your goals and how much pressure you like, then check in as I work. Deep pressure is never required: you can ask me to lighten up at any time, and I will. Research on deep tissue massage is limited and mixed. In a trial of 80 adults with neck pain linked to tender spots in the muscles, adding deep tissue massage to conventional rehabilitation was followed by more improvement in pain, quality-of-life scores and most neck movements than rehabilitation alone. [1] A larger trial of 619 adults with ongoing neck pain found that deep tissue massage led to more improvement in pain than advice to stay active in the short term but not by 12 months, and a review of the research found that studies differ too much in what they call deep tissue massage and how they do it to draw clear conclusions. [2] [3] People given massage, exercise or both in that larger trial were also more likely than those given advice to say they had recovered, at every follow-up through one year. [2] These are general findings, not medical advice or a promise of any result; the full summaries, including the weaker results, are in the research section below.
